title: Our Embodied Life, Part 2: Kisagotami and the Tender Heart
speaker: Ryushin Andrea Thach
summary: Ryushin Andrea Thach reads the story of Kisagotami from the children's book Siddhartha and the Swan, passing it around the room, then returns to the mustard seeds Kisa gathers house by house while looking for medicine for her dead son. Ryushin sets the story beside Siddhartha's first sight of old age, sickness and death, and beside the first abbess of San Francisco Zen Center, who started over after her heart attack and ended every conversation with "I love you." Ryushin draws on Christina Feldman's phrase "a state of argument with our lives," Stephen Batchelor's rendering of dukkha as life, and Issa's line "The dew drop world is the dew drop world." Participants answer with a mother's lost sense of special protection, a family member's mental illness, and the police shootings in the news that week.

sentences.text: Good evening, everyone.
This is week two of our four-week exploration of our embodied lives.
I realize today that all of these stories are told from the perspective of a woman.
We talked a little about that last week, but with the others, except this week, the theme is easily transferable.
Mahapajapati's fearlessness: you could imagine Mahatma Gandhi's fearlessness, or Martin Luther King's, or Rosa Parks's.
It's the same.
Those are names that easily pop to mind.
And next week you can also imagine that the story is particular to the gender it's being told from.
You could imagine the theme so easily being any person who is searching for their wholeness.
This one has, in some ways, the embodiment of a woman's body as particularly important, I think.
Not that it's not universal.
That's the theme.
It is universal.
But the subtitle for this is radical compassion, or the receptive heart, and this week, this last week particularly, has asked of us to look deeply in those ways.
So I thought, how lovely that this is a story of deep embodiment from a particular kind of experience, because it gives us an opportunity to explore that theme.
We'll see if that's what you think as we go through it.
I thought we would read it out loud, because it's always a nice way to enter into the story.
There are many different versions of this online, but I particularly thought we might enjoy reading the child's version.
There's a marvelous little book called Siddhartha and the Swan.
I have one copy, and I'll start it with Alice and pass it along.
Just read one paragraph or one part of the person speaking, and probably everyone will get a chance to speak, maybe more than once.
Kisa and the mustard seeds.
No, wait a minute.
Hand it back.
*Kisa grew up in an Indian village a long time ago, and she was quite young.
She got married and went to live with her husband's family in a town called Kapilavatthu.
When she first moved in with them, things were difficult.
She missed her village, her family, and her friends.
She felt that no one liked her and that everything she did was wrong.
Then when her son was born, everyone was very pleased and her life improved.
But when the baby was still tiny, her husband died.
Kisa was very upset.*
*Once that day, the baby also became very ill and died.
Kisa was so unhappy that she couldn't believe that her baby was dead.
She thought he must be asleep.
She wanted to end some, she wanted to find some special medicine that would make him better and begin asking everyone.
First she asked her neighbor, "Please, can you help me?"
She asked, "I need some special medicine for my baby."
"I'm sorry, Kisa," said the woman.
"I'm too busy to stop now.
Why don't you ask the storekeeper?"
Sadly, Kisa thanked her and went to the storekeeper.
But the storekeeper only told her to ask the doctor.
"Please, can you help me?"
Kisa asked the doctor.
"I need some special medicine for my baby."
The doctor looked at the baby in Kisa's arms.
He could see that it was dead.
"I'm sorry, Kisa," he said.
"I haven't got the medicine you need."
Was there anyone who could help Kisa, he wondered.
Then he remembered that the Buddha was staying nearby.
He was wise and very kind.
Maybe he would know how to help.*
*"Kisa," he suggested, "why don't you go and ask the Buddha?"
The Buddha was sitting in the shade of a tree talking to his friends when Kisa ran up to him.
He could see straight away that she was very upset.
"How can I help you?" he asked.
"My name is Kisa," she replied.
"I have been looking everywhere for medicine for my son."
The Buddha looked at the little bundle in Kisa's arms.
How could Kisa be helped to accept the truth that her little boy had really died?*
Judith, just pass it back around.
*"Kisa, if you want to make some medicine, you must have some mustard seeds," said the Buddha.
"Go into town and ask at each house.
But you must only accept seeds from a house in which no one has died."
Quickly, Kisa set off into town to get the mustard seeds.
At the first house, a young woman answered the door.
"Can I have some mustard seeds to make some medicine?"
Kisa asked.
Someone went back inside and soon returned with some seeds.
"Here you are," said the woman, smiling.*
*Kisa was just about to take the seeds when she remembered the Buddha's words.
"Oh, I nearly forgot," said Kisa.
"Has anyone died in this house?"
"Ah, yes," replied the young woman.
"A few months ago my grandmother died, very peacefully.
She was a lovely old lady and we remember her fondly.
But why, you ask."
"Thank you for getting me the seeds," said Kisa, "but I can only take them from a house in which nobody has died."
Kisa said goodbye and went to the next house.
An old man was sitting outside.
"Please, have you got some mustard seeds to spare?" she asked him.
Slowly the old man got up and went into the house.
Soon he emerged with some seeds.
"Here you are," said the woman, smiling.
Kisa was just about to take the seeds when she remembered the Buddha's words.*
I don't think so.
I think you went back.
You went back.
I think I really did.
*Again, just as Kisa was about to take the seeds she remembered what the Buddha had said.
"Has anyone in this house died recently?"
"Ah," replied the old man sadly.
"Just last year the lady at the house, my daughter, passed on.
We all still miss her."
"I am so sorry to hear your sad news," said Kisa.
"Thank you for getting me the seeds, but I'm afraid I can't take them after all."*
*At the next house she came to, a young boy entered the door.
"Please, have you got some mustard seeds to spare?" she asked.
"I'm sure we have," said the boy.
"Wait there and I'll ask my mom."
Soon the boy came back with the seeds.
"Here you are."
This time Kisa remembered.
"Can you tell me please if anyone has ever died in this house?" she asked.
"Yes," replied the boy quietly.
"When I was still a little baby, my dad died.
I can't even remember him."*
*"I'm sorry about your dad," said Kisa, "and thank you for getting me the seeds, but I cannot use them after all."
As Kisa went from door to door, the answer was the same.
Everyone had lost a loved one, if not last year, then a long time ago.
Kisa had no mustard seeds, but now she understood why she would not be able to hold any.
She looked at the little bundle in her arms.
"I'm sorry, my little one, you have gone to another life and I did not want to let you go.
Let us go and I'll find a resting place for you."
In the evening she returned to the Buddha.
She was no longer carrying the little bundle.
Her face was now much calmer.
"Have you been able to find the mustard seeds?"
Kisa asked.
"No," she replied, "but now I understand that everyone loses people they love.
I have laid my baby to rest and I'm now at peace.
Thank you."*
*"You have done well," said Kisa, said the Buddha, "for there is nothing stronger in all the world than a mother's love.
Would you like to stay with me for a while?"
As the sun went down over Kapilavatthu, Kisa and the Buddha talked.
She told him about her life and her baby.
He listened kindly.
The Buddha reminded Kisa that plants grow in the spring, flowers in the summer and die in the winter, and that new plants grow the following year.
Similarly, people are born and eventually die.
Kisa now understood that was just how things are.
Talking to the Buddha and listening to his kind words helped Kisa a lot.
That very evening she decided to become one of his followers.*
I've heard the story and told it many times, but it's strangely affecting, isn't it?
To hear it in so many voices, so many people talking in so many voices, I almost don't need to say anything.

Siddhartha, I'm going to go off script for a second and just say what comes to mind: seeing the seas of faces on all the videos this week of parents and mothers and brothers and sisters who have lost people to violence.
It's strangely affecting to hear this story in that context.
You'll see where I'm going with that.
When Siddhartha was a young man and left the palace for the first time, he saw old age, sickness and death.
They were strangers to him, and it set him on a path that brings us here today.
He wanted the answer, to try and make sense of all that.
It took him a good long time, and I'm impressed in this story that Kisatagami had this one experience and she, what did she see?
What did she really understand that led her to go against all convention, to shave her head and join an order just like that?
I think women give life, they carry life, life grows in them, they nurture, they attend death.
I think everyone has those capacities and those opportunities to do most of that, but it certainly is something that women know out of their bodies in a very intimate and fundamental, visceral way.
Maybe that's why she understood so immediately, when her grief opened a little bit, what her path was in response.
This story is usually taught as the universality of human existence.
Yes, that's what she found out.
Every door she knocked at, looking for those magic mustard seeds that would revive her baby, there was no house that hadn't experienced death, because it's a fundamental part of life.
In fact, the symbol of the mustard seed in this story: in India the mustard seed is the most common spice and it's the cheapest spice.
So what an apt symbol it is of that which you go looking for.

It should be the easiest thing to come by to cure life, but the cure, like so many things that you look for, looking for the answer, comes in a different form than what you ever would have imagined and maybe would have wanted.

In another version of this story, the introduction to it is that the man Kisatagami winds up marrying is the son of a rich man who is trying to sell his pile of ashes, which are really gold, and she's the only one who could see that actually those ashes are really valuable.
It's the symbolism of this story.
I think we get little inklings of this.
It's very hard to get.
For those of you who don't know, I'm a physician.

I take care of older people through stages of change and decrepitude and death, and it always amazes me how people will say, "I can't hike up Mount Baker anymore," or "it takes me, I don't know how long it should take."
How long does it take someone who's young and fit?
"It takes me twice as long as it used to.
I can't do it in the same way.
How can that be?
I can't get into the same yoga pose.
I've always gotten into it 70.
My toes turning up, right?"
But we do that.
"It's never been like this before."
That sense that we are somehow immutable and permanent.
The person with cancer who's clearly dying, who dies with chemotherapy running into their vein: it's very hard to accept that this precious, vital life actually comes to an end.
But Kisatagami saw it differently.

This weekend, the funeral of the first abbess of San Francisco's Zen Center was livestreamed, and someone reminded us that after her heart attack, which happened 20 years ago when she was 70, she said, "I need to start over.
I haven't really lived.
This is the only time I have.
I need to start over.
Every day really matters.
I need to live understanding that this doesn't go on and I'm not immune and the ones I love are not immune either."
Sometime after that, one of her early deshi's, a wonderful man named John King, died of AIDS.
She started every person that she met, every conversation she had, she ended it by saying, "I love you."
I think the story also is about radical acceptance.
It's not just that these things happen, okay, I'll buckle up to it.
It's that when the grief is too great to bear, the world no longer easily fits into our old ideas.
We're no longer the mother of a son who gives us status.
We're no longer a mother at all.
A college degree doesn't guarantee a secure job.
A professional life of good works doesn't promise special treatment.
Dharma practice doesn't guarantee happiness or an untroubled life, I hate to tell you.
But don't leave yet.
And a mother's love doesn't save a child from death.
When you really understand that you're not safe from anything, anything, where do you stand?
That's her example.

Christina Feldman in her commentary says, "Loss, death, and separation are real to us so poignantly that as long as we're malaligned with the core of the truth of impermanence, we live in a state of argument with our lives."
I think that's really wise.

As long as you're malaligned with loss, death, separation, separation from those you love, separation from your idea of yourself, separation from your opinions being true, separation from anything you identify with as me, mine, and myself, you don't actually understand that it's impermanent and not reality.
You live in a state of argument with your lives.
Oh, that's so tender, really, to miss out on your life because you're busy trying to make it into something that's not actually happening.
I can tell you I've spent the better part of 60 years doing that, wanting it to be different, thinking that I had some control over it.
Sometimes great, great grief, great loss is enough to shake us up to look and see beyond our control.
Something fundamental to who we think we are is stripped away, and it doesn't always turn out the way we want.
Sometimes we're lucky, sometimes our hard work gets us somewhere, but the world really turns on its own axis.
Going deeper, below that level, I think there's just human grief.
There's just the grief of loss.
There's just the grief of, oh, no.
There's just the grief of the 1929 stock market crash: oh, my whole life, my whole ability to provide, everything is gone.
There's just the grief of the tsunami waves hitting the shores of Irian Jaya, washing away hundreds of thousands of people.
There's just that grief.
Maybe there's nothing more personally strong than the grief of losing a child.
Loving in that way defines what life is about, that kind of bonding.
It's so fundamental to being human, to attach one to another.
But out of a deeply broken heart, an openness appears.
Or maybe it's a shattered heart, something that holds nothing and scatters it out and touches everything.
Broken open, at least to our own suffering, nothing can cover it.
No distractions of any kind.
The first noble truth, that there is suffering or unsatisfactoriness, is actually not accepting things as they are, period.
The suffering, I've always thought, is something extra that we add to the events of our life, or to what's happening around us, that makes the narrative of who we are.
You know, the storyline that says having a teen in trouble is like getting the feeling of payback for having been a bad kid yourself.
It's something extra.
Or events from years ago being the reasons for failures or problems now.
The problem now is just the problem now.
Or even standing in the grocery line thinking that the clerk is taking his time on purpose to make you late for your next event.
Right?
But in the context of this story, I think there's a more radical definition.
Stephen Batchelor translates dukkha not as suffering but as life.
Translating it as suffering or unsatisfactoriness in some ways makes it seem like, well, I can get out of that eventually, right?
All I need is to not be dissatisfied, just accept things really the way they are and it's all going to be okay.
But he says, uh-uh, it just goes along with the package.
We don't escape suffering.
The Zen stories are replete with great masters, such as Hakuin in The Hidden Lamp.
There's one about a great woman teacher, Sachu, about losing a child.
**Ryushin Andrea Thach:** Great masters on emptiness who believe in impermanence and lecture and really know those things, who fall apart, who wail and scream at the loss of their child.
They're great masters.
They know that life contains true feeling and suffering, that there's no escaping being human.
The 18th century Japanese haiku master Isa lost his baby daughter and wrote, *The dew drop world is the dew drop world.*
And yet, and yet, the dew drop world, the ephemeral world of change, everything reflected, everything changing.
And yet, and yet we live in it.
And yet we live with our feeling hearts, our bondedness to each other.
There's another story of Kisagotami that after this I don't need to read, but it goes on.
She actually loses everyone in her family and everything.
There's a stripping bare of her husband, of both of her children, of her family, of her family home.
In India, everyone has mustard seeds, and it flavors every food.
It's a tiny, tiny seed of potent flavoring.
In Christianity, some of you may know the story of the mustard seeds, an important parable.
And it's because the mustard grows big.
This story is a big story because it is, I think, the root of deep wisdom and radical compassion.
There are archival stories that we have in our culture.
I remember, dating myself to the 80s, Joseph Campbell's story of the hero, the archetypal stories of the hero.

That was one of the first times in this generation, this last 50 or 60 years, that the idea of everyone having their own mythic journey to find themselves was really something that people held up and talked about.
In a way, I think Kisagotami's journey through profound loss and pain to find her life again is our own mythic journey.
We see it in any deep loss we have: we have to come out and come home.
It's the opening for transcendent wisdom, anicca and anatta.
Nothing is permanent, no ideas, no person, no personality.
We all change over time, actually, and a body is mutable.

No self, we usually understand, is not separate, that they're interdependent with each other, that nothing happens in our life out of relationship with anyone else, and that the manifestation of this life, all the food that's gone into it, is the work of many people.

All the ideas that come out of this mouth are the training of many teachers, the writing of many people, all the wrinkles and pulled muscles, on and on and on, that our lives are totally interdependent.
Even speaking, we're creating this talk together.
It's that subtle and intimate constantly.
And that's a very good understanding.
But I think, radically, in reading this this time, preparing for this class, that it's even more than that.
That actually, they're not separate means that we're bound by the human feelings of vulnerability.
We're bound by the feelings of deep caring.
In Tibetan teachings, it's said that everyone has been everyone else's mother.
We've had so many lives.
And actually, it's really like that.
That teaching is really to remind us that it's really like that.
If we drop our ideas of our separate lives and taking care of me and mine, whether that's me or my family or my political party or my country boundaries or my...
If we really drop all of that, we realize we're all made of the same basic stuff and we operate in the same energetic, emotional feeling.

There's a lot of research that's done on the workings of the brain and the way the limbic system works, that we actually resonate with each other energetically and change each other's neurology, neurobiology.
But that's the root of radical compassion, that we actually are made of that stuff together.
I know you know it.
You've all had experiences like that.
I did in 1989 in the Loma Prieta earthquake in San Francisco.
You know those catastrophes where people realize how vulnerable it is and you walk down the street and everyone is available to each other completely.
How could you not watch the video of Diamond Reynolds narrating the death of her boyfriend, Philando Castillo, without feeling that?
Transcendent wisdom is the manifestation of fearlessness and of the receptive heart.
We need the fearless heart, the heart that feels deeply, that suffers in order not to turn away.
That heart can, as we said last week, still fear, still be afraid, still grieve deeply.
But out of our wisdom and out of our deep compassion, our deep understanding, because we too have suffered, we too know what loss is.
And we accept it as just what goes along with the package of being human.
It's nothing tragic.
It may be sad.
But it's part of what life is made of.
And actually there's a deep richness to accepting that that's what our life is made of, a deep richness.

I listened last night to another YouTube video of President Obama's speech, and I watched him say, in giving advice, how would it be if every policeman saw that young man who was being a young man, doing what young men do, messing up, saw every young man as his son, and the row of black mothers' heads behind him nodded.
What it would be like if we saw each other as each other's family.
It's not always possible.
We're human.
But it's what we're made of, actually.
It's really what we're made of.
Not because it's charitable or a bodhisattva act, but just because.
Just because.
So that's what I have to say.
That's the [unclear: "Phoenix box"].
And like last time, I wanted to ask how that lands for you.

What your experience, if you want to say something about the story or your relationship to it or what I said, or if you want to speak more personally about your experience of dealing with having things not be the way you wish they were or the way you hoped they were, or having your life turned inside out and how you met that.

**Participant:** That's what you said was very meaningful to me because I'm getting ready to have my 50th high school reunion, and you look at some of those faces, and they give you a list of the people that are around and the people that aren't.
That's loss.
Sometimes it doesn't make any sense.
I'm thinking about the woman.
She was moved by the Buddhist teaching to go from a relative truth about her own life, why me?
Why did this happen to me?
And then she discovered on her own, I think, an absolute truth that everything gets old, sick, or dies, which is kind of, in my mind, an absolute truth.
So I think there was something missing from the story.
If somebody can understand a basic truth on their own about a dying child, and I think back about all those other stories of people that were enlightened who were just holding up a flower.
In my mind, at that point, she was enlightened, but it isn't in the story that it should be.
**Ryushin Andrea Thach:** Please.
**Participant:** I'll share.
I had kind of an awakening.
I think I was 25 when I had my first child.
I think I still was in the world centered around me, and I was special.
I loved my daughter so much, I just was thinking that my love was going to protect her against anything.
Then I had a good friend whose child died.
I'm grateful it wasn't my child, but to have somebody close enough to you that you realized, I can't protect her.
My love isn't any more special than it.
And to think that that was an awakening for me, because I just sort of assumed that I was special and my love was so strong, and then you realize every mother's love is that, and you have no power.
The story just sort of brought that memory back.
I sort of forgot about that, having thought that.
Even though that was an awakening, it's happened again and again in littler ways, as you have real losses.
But the story's beautiful, and it's sad, and it's universal.
Thank you.
**Ryushin Andrea Thach:** Please.
**Participant:** This, to me, I feel like is the heart of our practice, and that's being with whatever it is that happens.
In my family, we have a person with mental illness, and we have all been on this journey, where he goes up and he comes down, and then he goes up and he comes down.
We keep planning on how we're going to help him, and if somehow he could just break through that place where he can accept his illness and take the medicine, and all of that.
And it's only been in recent times, I have to say part of it was my most recent dokusan.
It is as it is.
And he might not get better.
And even if he gets better, somebody else isn't going to get better.
Radical acceptance is to say, okay, we're here.
Thank you.
There's a lot of freedom in that place.
This may not be very coherent, what I'm going to say now, but I've been very moved by these acts of violence.
And in a way, police are our caregivers.
They show up when we're in trouble, when we have problems.
We call 911 when someone dies in an accident, and they show up.
And so in that way, this violation of our trust impacts even more than if it's just a thug killing somebody.
That's terrible.
And the person is just this [unclear: "bad bit"].
But we have the certain trust towards the police, or hope that they have justified trust.
And I've heard from the police department for more than a decade.
I frankly love these guys.
I've seen the other side.

I've seen a guy in his regular uniform getting dropped out of a helicopter into the Nooksack River to keep a suspect above water who jumped into the river to get away, and then in turn being in the hospital because of hypothermia and almost dying.
And I've seen them break down when shit happens to little kids.
And yet we say, we see what happens.
I firmly believe, unfortunately, that this is not something new.
It is just now technology and communication is at a point that the sheet that covered up all this stuff is getting pulled off.
And we're confronted by it, and we cannot avoid it.
And we still try, at least I am.
I'm going, oh, this is Chicago.
This is Dallas.
This is New York.
This is somewhere else.
But the Harvard University has this very interesting thing on its website.
It allows us to detect our bias towards all kind of minority groups.
And I've been living there for quite a while.
And I always thought I was okay.
I grew up in Germany.
I live in the United States.
My ex-husband was Mexican, Filipino.
I studied Japanese and from a Jewish teacher.
So I thought I was okay.
But you know what?
I'm biased.
And so is probably everybody else.
Even if we really try not to, even if our actions, if we don't act in a way that's biased, but we are always talking about other people and it happening in other places.
But it's happening right here.
We have an Hispanic community of migrant workers here in Bellingham.
There's a Russian community.
I never meet them.
And there is this separation.
How do we recognize the separation and the different communities?
How do we connect?
If anybody has any ideas, I'd be happy to listen.
**Participant:** Something else comes up for me in that that I just wanted to share.

In that video of Diamond Reynolds, the real FaceTime that was broadcast, what came across to me first was her extraordinary bravery to actually be broadcasting live in front of the cop who fired the gun, and her fear.
And also the enormous restraint on the part of that young man who was the cop who fired the shots.
I felt like I could see the fear in his face.
I felt like I could see the confusion.
What should I do here?
I could imagine the thoughts going through his mind.
Oh my God, all of this is being broadcast everywhere.
You know, someone who is really corrupt might have taken matters into his own hand.
He was a cop.
He could have gotten away with it.
He did not.
He restrained himself.
And I felt like I could see him really struggling.
And I appreciated the human emotion going on on everyone's part.
I saw that everyone was under enormous duress, suffering and working with it.
And we have our prejudices.
**Ryushin Andrea Thach:** We do.
We can't.
Take the Harvard.
Take the little tests.
You'll see.
We have our upbringing.
We have the ways, the causes and conditions that we bring to a circumstance.
What do we do with that?
How do we see each other?
How do we allow each other to come from the place they come from and to try and meet them the best we can?
That's our work.
I think that's what it really means to be compassionate.
Other people?
**Participant:** You used the term at the beginning, I think, the embodiment of our practice.
**Ryushin Andrea Thach:** Mm-hmm.
What do I mean by that?
**Participant:** Well, I was just feeling out in this story how after accepting her child's death and living a monastic life, Kisa continued grieving.
**Ryushin Andrea Thach:** Mm-hmm.
Mm-hmm.
I'm sure she didn't get away from it.
Thank you.
We're almost out of time.
Just want to see if there are any other feelings or thoughts that someone would like to...
**Participant:** This isn't really...

I don't have any real kind of direct experiences like this, but it's just, I guess, kind of going off the titles, or at least what I imagined you were about to say, because I guess it's kind of tumbling in my head.
Just how great a reminder this story is that the practice isn't there, or the practice isn't trying to eliminate or escape pain.
The pain is inevitable as part of life.
I'm really interested in Stephen Batchelor's ultimate translation of Dukkha.
I haven't heard of that before.
But instead, that we're not adding more suffering to the pain by not wanting to feel the pain.
I read somewhere someone described it as suffering twice for just one affliction.
And this is just a really good reminder that she didn't realize that everybody loses people and then not feel the pain anymore, but she wasn't.
She realized she didn't need to run from it.
It was really good.
Just sit with it.
Acceptance in that way.
This is really a powerful reminder of that.
Something else that came up as we were reading the story, put together into a coherent thing.
I don't have an ending from it, but it made me think of it as we were reading it.
The way we kind of hide our suffering in other people often is if we're ashamed of it, or we don't realize that everybody else is suffering just as much.
So we kind of add almost a third suffering to our stack.
Because we're feeling pain, and we don't want to feel it.
We have that sort of urge to get away from it, and then we have this feeling to hide it, which just has its own kind of level.
I feel like maybe in a way that's kind of what she was doing in the story, but not seeing it, she was denying it and suffering until she realized that everybody else also feels these same pains.
Really beautiful.
Thank you.
**Ryushin Andrea Thach:** John, do you want to have the last word?
**Participant:** Don't worry, I'll forget it.

What I thought about, a little bit related to what John said, one of the appeals of joining the Sangha of the Buddha is he could listen kindly and allow her to have her experience and feel her experience.
